stories.body: The US State Department has approved a possible $2.1bn sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 interceptor missiles, along with parts and support, to Ukraine. The purchase would be funded by contributions from Canada, Germany and Norway and EU-backed financing, rather than US funds. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy welcomed the decision but said Ukraine needs interceptors immediately as Russia intensifies attacks on energy infrastructure; the missiles are newly manufactured and may not arrive until the early 2030s unless existing US stocks can be made available sooner.
stories.headline: US approves $2.1bn sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine

stories.body: Hundreds of civilians have been evacuated from the devastated Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky under a localized ceasefire and humanitarian operation brokered with US involvement. Twenty-five buses and ambulances were sent to bring food, medicine and residents out of the city, where shortages of essentials have become severe. Evacuees heading to Ukrainian-controlled territory are to travel through Russian-held territory to Anapa, fly to Belarus and then cross into Ukraine, while several hundred residents, many of them older people, chose to remain.
stories.headline: Rare ceasefire enables civilian evacuation from Russian-occupied Oleshky

stories.body: Novaya Gazeta, Russia's best-known independent newspaper, says it will permanently close after more than three decades, citing the loss of its newsroom, publishing license and donation platforms amid intensified state pressure. The paper, long known for investigations into corruption and human-rights abuses, had continued operating in limited form after Russia's invasion of Ukraine despite censorship laws, website blocks and foreign-agent designations. Six of its journalists have been killed over the years, including Anna Politkovskaya; co-founder and Nobel Peace Prize winner Dmitry Muratov said authorities had chosen to "strangle" the outlet.
stories.headline: Russia's Novaya Gazeta announces closure amid escalating Kremlin pressure

stories.body: Nearly 200 countries meeting in Yerevan approved two agreements intended to accelerate implementation of the 2022 Global Biodiversity Framework, which commits nations to halt and reverse nature loss by 2030. Delegates acknowledged that progress is badly behind schedule, with the UN saying the world is on track to meet only one of the framework's 24 targets. Countries pledged more than $1bn during the meeting and made progress on addressing environmentally harmful subsidies, but the central financing gap remains: a previous commitment to provide $30bn annually for nature recovery by the end of the decade is not being met at the required pace.
stories.headline: Nearly 200 countries approve biodiversity agreements, but funding remains unresolved

stories.body: The US cancelled the traditional G20 foreign ministers' family photo in Atlanta after the UK, Australia, EU countries and other delegations said they would not appear beside Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov. About one-third of participants were reportedly unwilling to join the photograph, and US officials said cancelling it avoided turning a ceremonial event into a diplomatic distraction. The dispute reflected continuing divisions over Russia's invasion of Ukraine, with British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband directly accusing Russia of being the aggressor and of killing civilians.
stories.headline: G20 family photo cancelled after countries refuse to appear alongside Russia

stories.body: Iran's Revolutionary Guards said four oil tankers had been struck and were on fire in the Strait of Hormuz, while President Donald Trump said the war with Iran would be resolved soon. The reports come amid sharply mixed signals from Washington and Tehran: US military planners have reportedly briefed Trump on options for renewed attacks and shifted air defenses and munitions in the region, while Vice President JD Vance has sought direct talks with Iranian officials through Qatari mediators. Analysts say the parallel military preparations and diplomatic outreach underline the lack of trust and uncertainty over whether the conflict is headed toward a renewed offensive or negotiations.
stories.headline: Iran says four oil tankers are on fire in the Strait of Hormuz as diplomacy and escalation signals collide

stories.body: Republican officials and strategists are increasingly worried that an already difficult midterm environment could produce losses in districts and states once considered safely Republican. Concerns center on high living costs, fuel prices, the Iran war and weak turnout among some Trump supporters, while party committees have expanded spending and polling into redder territory. Internal anxiety extends to House races and Senate contests in states including Ohio, Kansas, South Carolina and Louisiana, though public and private polls in many competitive races remain close and Republican leaders reject the pessimistic assessment.
stories.headline: Republicans brace for potentially severe midterm losses in traditionally safe territory

stories.body: Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed's campaign has asked former primary rival Rep. Haley Stevens not to attend further campaign events in the final days before the election, exposing continuing divisions in a pivotal race. Stevens had said she would campaign with El-Sayed but wanted him to apologize for past comments and condemn an outside advertisement she called antisemitic; El-Sayed responded by urging Democrats to focus on defeating Republican Mike Rogers. The seat being vacated by Sen. Gary Peters is central to Democratic hopes of winning Senate control, and party figures warned that the public dispute could damage turnout and unity.
stories.headline: Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed asks Haley Stevens to stay off the campaign trail

stories.body: Democratic lawmakers, strategists and pollsters caution that likely midterm gains would primarily reflect backlash to President Trump rather than a repaired party brand or a durable governing message. They point to weak party approval ratings, lingering factional divisions and a continuing struggle to persuade voters that Democrats can manage the economy and lower everyday costs. While candidates have rallied around attacks on Republican "costs, chaos and corruption," some party figures argue Democrats will need a clearer positive agenda and tangible results if they regain congressional power and hope to win the presidency in 2028.
stories.headline: Democrats warn a favorable midterm could mask unresolved weaknesses ahead of 2028

stories.body: A new Politico poll conducted by PF Global found that only 25% of Americans believe political surveys accurately estimate election results, reflecting broad distrust across party lines ahead of the midterms. Many Republicans believe polls undercount their party, an opinion shaped in part by polling errors during the Trump era, while substantial numbers of Democrats also believe their side is underestimated. Pollsters say surveys are snapshots rather than predictions and acknowledge that declining response rates and last-minute voter shifts make their work more difficult, but argue that polling remains a useful tool when conducted rigorously.
stories.headline: Only one in four Americans trusts political polls to estimate election results accurately

stories.body: Spain's investigation into the Urda high-speed rail collision is examining the repeated failure of the LZB automatic safety system and instructions issued by the Adif control center in Atocha. The system reportedly failed 170 times this year, and after its failure on the Madrid-Seville line, the AVE was reportedly authorized to resume normal speed rather than proceed under the low-speed visual-driving protocol. The AVE subsequently struck a stopped Iryo train at more than 160 km/h, killing at least 69 people; recordings and official accounts indicate controllers knew the Iryo remained stationary, while the minister said investigators must determine why the AVE was not stopped.
stories.headline: Urda train-crash investigation focuses on safety-system failures and the control-center response

stories.body: Transport Minister Óscar Puente says the government is considering a full closure of the Madrid-Barcelona high-speed rail line for between 12 and 24 months to complete major renewal works, rather than carrying them out around operating services over roughly five years. The option would affect Spain's busiest high-speed route, used by about 40,000 passengers a day, but could improve reliability and punctuality and allow a more comprehensive upgrade. Puente said the review was not a direct response to the Urda crash, but that recent accidents and service disruptions had prompted wider reflection on the quality and dependability of the rail system.
stories.headline: Spain considers closing Madrid-Barcelona high-speed line for up to two years for renewal work

stories.body: Spain's Supreme Court has admitted 69 individuals and three organizations as affected parties in the case that suspended voting rights for more than 163,000 people naturalized under the country's Democratic Memory, or "grandchildren's," law. The court has opened a three-day period for submissions, including on a request by the party Iustitia Europa to extend the suspension to the children of people naturalized under the law. The dispute concerns allegations of an irregular expansion of the electoral roll; people who have certified that they are children or grandchildren of political exiles remain eligible to vote.
stories.headline: Spanish Supreme Court admits 69 people and three groups into case over descendants' voting rights

stories.body: Spanish authorities have arrested at least eight young people, including an alleged 20-year-old founder of the online Blocus movement, over alleged efforts to organize looting and unrest during Halloween. Investigators say the suspect administered Telegram groups used to coordinate disturbances and share instructions for raids on businesses, while another arrest involved messages encouraging the making of Molotov cocktails. The operation follows looting and vandalism in Barcelona on October 24 and comes amid concern that new calls for disorder could lead to incidents in cities including Barcelona and Valencia.
stories.headline: Spanish police arrest alleged Blocus founder ahead of expected Halloween unrest

stories.body: Catalonia's competition authority has urged Barcelona to preserve private shared-bike services rather than allow their licenses to expire in 2027, warning that eliminating them would reduce transport choices and weaken pressure on the city-run Bicing system to improve prices, quality and innovation. The authority called for new rules that allow public and private operators to coexist, noting the city is both regulator and owner of Bicing. City officials say they are reviewing the recommendation but maintain that non-renewal is justified by repeated breaches of license conditions and the impact of poorly parked bikes on public space.
stories.headline: Catalonia's competition authority urges Barcelona to preserve private shared-bike services

stories.body: Barcelona's juvenile prosecutor has requested supervised release and nationwide bans on attending demonstrations or other gatherings for 70 minors arrested in connection with looting and unrest in the city last weekend, and has sought detention for eight of them. Police arrested 89 minors among 130 people detained during the incidents, which also prompted around 30 fire-service calls. Mossos d'Esquadra have since detained several more young people suspected of organizing or promoting Blocus channels that allegedly coordinated looting, disorder and violence against police, while authorities maintain heightened vigilance for Halloween.
stories.headline: Barcelona prosecutors seek protest bans for 70 minors arrested in recent looting
